title: Longitudinal Serum Proteomics in Hypertensive Kidney Disease Progression
projectDescription: Hypertensive nephrosclerosis (HN) is a major cause of end-stage renal disease (ESRD), however, longitudinal studies employing serum proteomics to document its progression are few. This study aims to identify potential circulating biomarkers indicative of disease progression in HN by performing serum proteomic analysis at two time points in patients with progressive and stable disease courses.
sampleProcessingProtocol: Serum samples (10 µL each) were thawed on ice. Protein depletion was carried out using Protein Depletion Mini Spin Columns. 40 µL of protease inhibitor in water and 4 µL of 100 µM dithiothreitol was added. After incubation, 6 µL of freshly prepared 200 µM iodoacetamide was added. SP3 method was used for protein isolation. Digestion was performed using 50 µL of digestion solution (100 mM ammonium bicarbonate/1 mM calcium chloride) containing a 1:25 enzyme-to-protein ratio of trypsin. Samples were desalted. Proteomics were performed using tandem mass tag (TMT) labelling and liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS).
dataProcessingProtocol: Processing of raw mass spectrometric data was performed using Proteome Discover Software (Thermo-Fisher). Mass spectra were searched against the human Universal Protein Resources (UniProt). Further processing of the proteomic data was perfromed in R (v 4.4.1). Peptides with over 50% zero abundance across all samples and potential contaminants, like keratins and bovine serum peptides, were removed. The top 14 most abundant serum and red blood cell proteins were also excluded before the differential expression analysis (Table S1). Missing peptide values resulting from batch effects were imputed using random forest regression through the missForest (v 1.5.0) package. The imputation was performed group-wise, based on protein levels within the respective groups. In instances where there were too few peptides available in a single group to apply regression, mean imputation was used instead.    Differential expression was performed using LIMMA (v 3.60.3). Batch correction was performed using LIMMA’s removeBatchEffect function.
